::: {.visual-explainer .explainer-repair}


I test whether a correction learned for one fine-tuned model can help repair another. As in
[Selective editing](../selective-editing/explainer.qmd), I deliberately worsen predictions in one language
and measure the side effects on another.

Here I fine-tune [Goodfire's four-layer, 67-million-parameter language model](https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters)
by training updates to its 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices. The training objective pushes
**German prediction loss up** while penalizing changes to English, French, Spanish and Italian predictions,
leaving Dutch unprotected during fine-tuning.

The model shares weights across languages, so the German edit can also affect Dutch. In these runs, Dutch
prediction loss increases relative to the base model. This increase is the **Dutch damage** to be repaired.
A **repair** is an additional weight change trained to restore Dutch prediction quality while keeping the
intended German change.

On two new fine-tunes, the earlier repair was most useful **as a starting point when fitting data and steps
were limited**. Rescaling its fixed directions left more Dutch damage. Allowing those directions to adapt
removed almost all of it. At the full fitting budget, a new repair learned from scratch nearly caught up.

## Training the repair {#the-same-starting-repair-two-ways-to-reuse-it}

The earlier fine-tune is the **donor** and its correction is the **donor repair**. The **primary target** is
the first new fine-tuned model I repair. I repeat the comparison on a second model, the **replication target**.
All three models are fine-tuned separately from the same base model, using the same recipe with different
seeds and samples from the same distribution of European Parliament text (Europarl).

To learn a repair, I hold the fine-tuned model's weights fixed and train an added update to match the base
model's next-token probabilities on Dutch while keeping the fine-tuned model's predictions on German and
the four other languages. I first learn the donor repair from scratch, then reuse that same repair for
both targets.

Each repair adds a **rank-one update**, formed from an input and an output vector, to each of 24 weight
matrices. I compare **three ways to train the repair**:

1. **Scalar coefficients only:** keep the donor's vectors fixed and learn one scalar coefficient per matrix.
2. **Donor initialization:** start from the donor's vectors and train both on the new fine-tune.
3. **Fresh initialization:** start with random input vectors and zero output vectors, then train both.

The fresh start tests whether the donor provides a useful head start over learning a new correction.

## Changing the directions repairs more damage {#keeping-the-directions-leaves-damage-behind}

For each target, scalar-only fitting learns **24 multipliers for the donor repair**, one per weight matrix.
The donor's input and output vectors stay fixed. Each target gets its own fitted multipliers.
Here **recovery** is the share of the fine-tune's extra Dutch prediction loss removed:
100% restores the base model's Dutch loss.

For each method and budget, I choose a checkpoint—a repair saved during training—on separate selection
text, taking the one that recovers the most Dutch damage while passing the checks on German and the other
languages. I then evaluate that repair on 92 Europarl session dates held out of both repair fitting and selection.

At the full fitting budget, scalar coefficients recover about **87%** on the first target and **78%** on the
second. Donor initialization recovers about **98–99%**. All full-budget repairs shown preserved the German
effect and met the constraints on the other languages.

```{=html}

  <figcaption id="repair-full-caption">Full budget: 2,048 fit tokens, with checkpoints selected from runs of up to 600 steps.
  Scalar-only selection also considers two extra runs per target that optimize the coefficients until convergence.
  Whiskers show 95% bootstrap intervals
  over 92 Europarl evaluation dates.</figcaption>
</figure>
<p id="repair-primary-result" class="explainer-finding">Donor initialization exceeds the scalar-coefficient fit by 11.3 percentage
points on the first target and 20.4 points on the second.</p>
```

<details class="visual-details">
<summary>How the scalar coefficients were fitted</summary>

To check whether the scalar fit simply needed more optimization, I ran two additional searches for each
target. One starts from the donor repair, scaled down if its weight norm exceeds the fine-tune's. The other
starts from the ordinary checkpoint with the lowest fitting loss. Like ordinary training, both use all
2,048 fitting tokens at each step, but continue until further updates make negligible progress under the
study's stopping rules.

The regular search saves a checkpoint every 50 steps up to step 600 at each of four learning rates, giving
48 checkpoints. The two extra results join these in the selection pool. A separate selection set chooses
the repair shown above. On the primary target, an ordinary checkpoint is still selected (**86.9% recovery**).
On the replication target, one of the extra runs is selected (**78.4%**, compared with **77.3%** from the
ordinary search). The larger search still leaves a recovery gap. It does not rule out every other choice
of coefficients.

</details>

## The donor helps most when fitting is constrained

To find out when the earlier repair is useful, I compare all three training methods at different
amounts of fitting data and training steps.

The fitting budget counts distinct prediction positions across Dutch, German and the four other languages.
For a given budget, all methods reuse the same fitting text at every step.

With **256 fit tokens and up to 50 steps**, starting from the donor recovers about **4 percentage points**
more Dutch damage than fresh initialization. With **2,048 tokens and up to 600 steps**, fresh fitting nearly
catches up: the donor's lead is **1.1–1.4 points**, with both 95% intervals entirely inside the study's
**±2-point band for practical equivalence**.

In the regular search, scalar-only recovery changes little across these budgets: **86.9–87.4%** on the primary target and
**76.3–77.4%** on the replication target.
